entry.summary: 2 minute read Insta360 Ace Pro 3, Osmo Action 7 release date 2:43 Insta360's Ace Pro 3 might have FCC approval, but Simon Wyndham still expects it and DJI's Action 7 to wait until spring 2027. We've been spoiled this year. There has been a run of strong action camera releases, in
entry.content:
2 minute read
Insta360 Ace Pro 3, Osmo Action 7 release date
2:43

Insta360's Ace Pro 3 might have FCC approval, but Simon Wyndham still expects it and DJI's Action 7 to wait until spring 2027.

We've been spoiled this year. There has been a run of strong action camera releases, including a whole new platform from GoPro, the gimbal camera wars between Insta360 and DJI, and plenty more.

When the rumor mill kicked into high gear around the Insta360 Ace Pro 3 and the rumored DJI Osmo Action 7, it was easy to assume the launches were imminent.

However, Simon Wyndham thinks differently, and he presents a compelling case for why the reality might be otherwise.

In short, he argues that a busy year and Christmas discounting make a 2026 release improbable. He also says he has not been briefed on either camera, which he would expect ahead of a pre-Christmas launch. For all the stop-start release shenanigans this year, journalists and the channel were all primed to go in the background. Releasing two major cameras cold would be a brave move. His prediction isn’t even a Q1 2027 release for the new cameras, but a Q2 one.

Likely features and capabilities

On the much-rumored one-inch sensors, he reckons both companies face the close focus and hyperfocal distance problems that affected GoPro's Mission 1 Pro. He notes that DJI's Action 6 addressed this with a mechanical iris that stops down to f4, which reduces the benefit of a larger sensor. He suggests Insta360 might skip the larger sensor unless it adopts a mechanical iris, and says bigger sensors would also mean bulkier lenses, complicating wide-angle and boost lens attachments.

Could the Ace Pro 3 and Action 7 shift toward vlogging, leaving helmet and body mounting to smaller cameras such as Insta360's Go Ultra and DJI's Osmo Nano? It's possible.

Log profiles, frame rates, and batteries

Moving on to the wish list, he hopes DJI offers full D-Log rather than D-Log M, expects 10-bit I-Log from Insta360, and would like Insta360's Cine Look modes combined with I-Log. On slow motion, he reports rumors of 240 fps on the Action 7 and 120 fps on the Ace Pro 3, and expects the Ace Pro 3 to stay at 120 fps. He considers 8K60 a likely addition, and he reckons the Action 7 will keep DJI's shared battery system and the Ace Pro 3 will keep its own.

Finally, he considers dual lenses and Lidar unlikely. But given that we're already well into November and steaming towards the end of the year, it won't be too long before we know for sure

entry.title: Cinema lenses: why glass still matters
entry.summary: 3 minute read Cinema lenses: why glass still matters 4:31 Replay: Despite all the changes in the past 10 years, good glass is still resisting commoditization and is as important as ever. [This article was first published in September 2016 and has been updated. Ed] Lenses remain f
entry.content:
3 minute read
Cinema lenses: why glass still matters
4:31

Replay: Despite all the changes in the past 10 years, good glass is still resisting commoditization and is as important as ever.

[This article was first published in September 2016 and has been updated. Ed]

Lenses remain firmly in the analog domain. They also remain in the "they cost quite a lot of money" domain. That's because making glass lenses isn't subject to Moore's Law, or any other phenomenon that would constantly drive prices down. Making lenses is labor-intensive, and there's no easy way to reduce this.

But if you're prepared to pay the price for a good cinema prime or zoom lens, you're in for a treat, because not all lenses are the same.

This article was initially published a decade ago, just after IBC2016 in Amsterdam, where we visited several cinema lens manufacturers in quick succession. There's an endemic difficulty for lens makers: their products look superficially similar, both physically and optically, if you're not looking very closely or don't know much about lenses.

Every lens range has its own look

There have been many changes in the 10 years since, not least the avalanche of low-cost and very capable lenses from a host of Chinese manufacturers that has reshaped the market for glass.

But even there at the value end of the market, look a bit deeper and every range of lenses has some pretty unique characteristics. Some might be clinically clean, with minimal distortion and strikingly good sharpness. Others might go for a look that, depending on its nature, can help cinematographers get closer to the final appearance they had in mind for the film.

Some lens manufacturers deliberately engineer a look. Sometimes this is achieved through imperfections. Occasionally the look is engineered to, for example, give a better-looking and more pronounced bokeh.

There are as many looks as there are types of lens. This could be an issue, but it's mitigated by the fact that a set of cinema primes will probably be so well matched that the lenses are easily interchangeable.

With the ability to choose a look that is generated by your lens, you're less likely to need to apply looks in post-production, although some would see the lens look as a basic starting point for later modification.

What really matters is that when you apply a look in the analog domain, you are likely to retain the full information in the image. It's a critical part of the acquisition process, and it's where lens manufacturers try their hardest to distinguish their products from everyone else's.

The main lens looks

There's the clean, ultra-sharp, precision look, for when you want your lens to simply capture everything that's there.

There's the warm, somewhat soft but engaging look for shots that don't need the ultimate in sharpness but call for a gentler, less stark appearance.

And there's the look designed to emphasize the out-of-focus areas of the image, giving as smooth a bokeh as is physically possible.

Most lenses also have a characteristic color temperature. Cooler lenses tend to be more scientifically clinical and might be better suited to shooting machinery or urban scenes. Warmer lenses are kinder to skin tones. As always, there are exceptions: dystopian sci-fi might feature a lot of flesh, but with a blue/silver metallic hue.

Ultimately, it's all subjective, but that makes it no less important. Cinematographers and DOPs choose lenses based on their look and, hence, largely on their emotional response to the images.

How much of the look can post replace?

Since this was first written, post has caught up in some ways. ZEISS eXtended Data, launched in 2017, builds on Cooke /i metadata to pass shading and distortion data into post, and ZEISS CinCraft LensCore, a Nuke plugin, simulates the bokeh, defocus, distortion, and vignetting of specific lenses. Simulation is still not the same as glass, but the gap is smaller than it was in 2016.

It's tempting to say that the lens is the most important part of the camera, optically and in terms of the look. Superficial similarity in appearance shouldn't mask the important differences between lenses, some intentional and some accidental. Whatever the cause, there's more choice than ever, at low and high budgets.

So don't assume the look is always achievable in post. It's usually better to get it right in the lens. Nature is analog, and so are lenses. It's a perfect match.

entry.title: Star Trek TNG remaster: why DS9 never got one
entry.summary: 2 minute read Star Trek TNG remaster: why DS9 never got one 4:40 CBS rebuilt every episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation from its original film. But disappointing sales left Deep Space Nine and Voyager in standard definition. Star Trek turned 60 on September 8, and Paramount
entry.content:
2 minute read
Star Trek TNG remaster: why DS9 never got one
4:40

CBS rebuilt every episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation from its original film. But disappointing sales left Deep Space Nine and Voyager in standard definition.

Star Trek turned 60 on September 8, and Paramount marked the date with restored 4K screenings of classic films in more than 750 US theaters. One of the franchise’s best restorations, though, Star Trek: The Next Generation, is older, and was made for a much smaller screen. We were reminded of it when revisiting old episodes to mark the sad death of Sir Patrick Stewart last week.

CBS announced its Blu-ray remaster of The Next Generation, starring Sir Patrick as Captain Picard, in September 2011, on the show’s 24th anniversary. Over a decade later, it remains one of the benchmarks for restoring a television series that was shot on film but finished on video.

Glorious (re)master (re)visited

We covered this a decade ago in a piece written for Star Trek’s 50th anniversary. The show was shot on 35mm film with Panavision cameras and lenses, but its edits and effects were done on standard-definition videotape, which held back the quality of the broadcast version. The restoration went back to the original film and audio elements, scanned them, and rebuilt each episode as originally broadcast. The result was a 1080p picture with DTS-HD Master Audio 7.1 sound.

Every episode had to be reconstructed from the original film, with the broadcast video edits as a guide. That meant finding and scanning each take, plus every effects element layered on top of it, from the model passes to the lights and the star field.

So, where’s the rest?

Robert Meyer Burnett, who produced special features for the Blu-ray sets, has put the cost of the Next Generation restoration at somewhere north of $12 million. Back in 2017 he estimated that remastering Deep Space Nine and Voyager would cost around $20 million per series, roughly $40 million in total, and take about eight years.

Problem one is the vfx. Both shows moved to CGI partway through, with the elements spread across several effects houses and some possibly lost entirely. And those that remained would be SD shots, meaning that the majority of the vfx would have to be rebuilt from scratch.

Problem two is that the disc sales of the TNG remasters did not match projections, which he put down to the high price of the early seasons at close to $120 a set and the shift to streaming. And if those economics were a problem in 2017, you can bet they’re even less attractive now. Skydance, which owns Paramount and with it the current rights to Star Trek, completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6 and carries roughly $80 billion in debt.

A decade on, the picture has barely moved. The Original Series films were remastered in 4K in 2021 and 2022, and the four Next Generation films followed in April 2023. Neither DS9 nor Voyager yet has an official HD release at the time of writing. Paramount’s 60th anniversary Original Series Blu-ray set contains no new 4K remaster of the episodes.

Fans have not waited. Billy Reichard’s AI-upscaled clips of Voyager and DS9 drew wide coverage when they were first released six years ago. His new ones are even better as the latest clip of Star Trek Voyager S02E18 Death Wish shows.

And the 2018 documentary What We Left Behind remastered 30 minutes of DS9 from the original negatives with CBS Digital, in an attempt to make the case for the whole show. Even if Paramount is skint, you would think that a combination of a long-tail Trek fanbase reachable easily via a global streaming service and the improvement in AI tools, especially when it comes to upscaling even those tricky vfx shots, might change the equations the accounts department is looking at.

Great work, Scotty

We touched on the DS9 and Voyager issue in a 2020 article titled prosaically This is why you might never see your favourite TV shows remastered, and one of the comments gave us possibly the most elegant solution to the problem we’ve come across.

“Actually, remastering Deep Space Nine would be a simple process. Just put it into the transporter buffer, have the main computer reconfigure all the clips as necessary, and then beam the processed video directly to Ops,” wrote commenter Ferris Akel III. Sounds like a plan.

entry.title: OBSBOT Meet Flip long-term review: foldable 4K webcam
entry.summary: 2 minute read OBSBOT Meet Flip long-term review: foldable 4K webcam 3:53 The $119 OBSBOT Meet Flip folds shut to cover the lens and enter sleep mode. Image quality rivals pricier OBSBOT models, but the mics are average. OBSBOT built its name on gimbaled PTZ cameras and AI auto-fr
entry.content:
2 minute read
OBSBOT Meet Flip long-term review: foldable 4K webcam
3:53

The $119 OBSBOT Meet Flip folds shut to cover the lens and enter sleep mode. Image quality rivals pricier OBSBOT models, but the mics are average.

OBSBOT built its name on gimbaled PTZ cameras and AI auto-framing, so a $119 fixed webcam looks like a step down on paper. In practice, the Meet Flip is one of the more sensible things the company has released. It strips away the pan, tilt, and zoom hardware and keeps the sensor, the software, and a useful piece of mechanical design.

Fold-to-close privacy hinge

The headline feature is right there in the name. The camera body hinges into its own desk mount, and closing it physically covers the lens while dropping the device into sleep mode. It replaces the usual routine of a sliding plastic cap or even a strip of tape over the lens with something that is impossible to misjudge from across a room: open means live, closed means dark. OBSBOT frames this as privacy you don't have to think about, and for once the marketing line and the hardware match. The mic is disabled whenever the lens is folded shut.

I've been using it for several months now and it has become my go-to webcam. I prefer it even to gimbaled models, which can inadvertently reveal a less-than-tidy office if I get up from my desk during a meeting.

Meet Flip specs: sensor, video modes, and size

Specs are respectable for the price. The Meet Flip uses a 1/2-inch stacked CMOS sensor (Sony Exmor RS architecture with Quad Bayer processing) at 48 megapixels effective, with an f/1.8 aperture and phase-detect autofocus. It shoots 4K30 or 1080p60, with a 72-degree field of view in 16:9. HDR is supported but shipped off by default, and has to be switched on in OBSBOT Center.

Digital zoom goes up to 4x, defaulting to 2x out of the box. Autofocus can be disabled in favor of manual control through the same software.

Weight is 37.7 g (1.33 oz), and the body measures roughly 42 x 37 x 32 mm (1.65 x 1.46 x 1.26 in). The integrated mount clips to a laptop or monitor bevel and carries a 1/4-20 UNC tripod thread, with landscape, portrait, and upside-down orientation support. Connectivity is USB-C.

Image quality, audio, and AI framing in use

Image quality is great and well up there with the pricier OBSBOT Tiny 3 despite the smaller sensor. You could use it for anything from meetings to full-on content creation with confidence. The audio implementation is perhaps less successful. Built-in mics with four modes (directional mode for solo calls, dual-directional for two-person interviews, a smart omni mode for group meetings around a table, and a pure/unprocessed stereo option) are okay for meetings, but not a reason to ditch an external mic for anything audience-facing.

If there is a frustration, it is that the AI auto-framing can be a bit intrusive and gesture control can toggle things on (or off) far too easily. And yes, I did toggle gesture control off: it's just willfully persistent in coming back. As with Insta360 and other webcams, there's also a subscription real-time transcription service that will generate transcripts and meeting notes, though I've yet to find one that presents a meaningful leap in quality over the alternatives.

Pricing and availability

At $119, the Meet Flip undercuts OBSBOT's own Meet 2 while matching its sensor size and resolution, and it's a smart pickup for anyone whose current webcam is a laptop's built-in camera or an aging 1080p USB unit. And that privacy hinge is a pleasingly low-tech and definitive solution for anyone who has not always been quite sure that off is really off.

entry.title: Adobe Premiere mobile adds UMG and WMG licensed music
entry.summary: 1 minute read Adobe Premiere mobile adds UMG and WMG licensed music 1:43 Adobe's free Premiere mobile app is getting licensed Universal and Warner music. Clips run to 60 seconds for personal, non-commercial use only. Adobe has announced it is working with two of the world's bigge
entry.content:
1 minute read
Adobe Premiere mobile adds UMG and WMG licensed music
1:43

Adobe's free Premiere mobile app is getting licensed Universal and Warner music. Clips run to 60 seconds for personal, non-commercial use only.

Adobe has announced it is working with two of the world's biggest music companies, Universal Music Group (UMG) and Warner Music Group (WMG), to bring fully licensed music clips from leading artists into its free video editing app, Adobe Premiere mobile.

Adobe says users will be able to browse, search, and preview trending music by artist or track, filter by genre and duration, bookmark favorites, and explore music through label-featured collections. The features are coming soon, though no timing has been given.

Up to 60 seconds of a track can be added to a video. Customizable templates paired with music will also be available, and finished videos can be exported and posted to licensed social platforms.

Here's the big caveat: tracks from UMG and WMG are licensed for personal, non-commercial use. Adobe Stock Audio remains available for projects that require commercially licensed music. Plus, we as yet have no idea of the size and depth of these libraries, or indeed whether any artists have carve-outs that preclude their music from featuring in such deals. The catalogs, though, suggest Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish, Muse, Nirvana, and many, many more.

Sony, the third of the big three, isn't mentioned in the announcement. CapCut and Instagram Edits already draw on major-label catalogs through their parent companies' licensing deals, so this is Adobe catching up. But it puts Adobe alongside two widely used editing apps and, as a gateway to the wider Adobe ecosystem, it makes sound commercial sense.

entry.summary: 1 minute read Pro Tools 2026.11: Extensions, Stem Separator, MPE 2:29 Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, adding a third-party Extensions format and an AI Stem Separator. MPE support and Windows High DPI scaling also arrive. Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, which adds a new
entry.content:
1 minute read
Pro Tools 2026.11: Extensions, Stem Separator, MPE
2:29

Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, adding a third-party Extensions format and an AI Stem Separator. MPE support and Windows High DPI scaling also arrive.

Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, which adds a new plugin format called Pro Tools Extensions, an AI-powered Stem Separator, MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE), and Windows improvements.

Extensions add third-party tools

Unlike traditional AAX plugins, which operate on individual tracks, Extensions can support processes spanning multiple tracks or entire sessions. They are accessed from the Pro Tools Edit window. Partners at launch include Pro Sound Effects and Soundly (sound effects libraries), Forte (track importing, organization, and delivery), and Pibox (collaboration and feedback). The existing Splice and SoundFlow integrations from 2025 will also be available as Extensions, including their AI-enabled capabilities.

AI Stem Separator

The Pro Tools Stem Separator Extension separates recordings into up to six stems: vocals, drums, bass, guitar, keys, and other. It works without exporting files to external applications or uploading audio to cloud services. Users drag audio into the Extension, preview the stems, and bring them back into the session as individual tracks. It is included at no additional cost with all versions of Pro Tools, including the free Pro Tools Intro.

MPE and Windows updates

MPE lets individual notes respond independently to gestures such as pressure and pitch movement, whereas in conventional MIDI changes like pitch bend typically affect multiple notes at once. It requires compatible controllers and virtual instruments, and also allows real-time manipulation of timbre, filters, and effects.

On Windows, the release adds High DPI support for 2K, 4K, and 8K monitors, per-monitor scaling, enhanced compatibility scaling, and improved dark theme support for title bars, menus, and common dialogs. Playlist Clip Color Coding gives consistent colors across tracks for different takes.

Availability and upgrades

Pro Tools 2026.11 is available now to Pro Tools Artist, Studio, and Ultimate subscribers, perpetual license holders with an active upgrade plan, and Pro Tools Intro users. All major new enhancements are supported across Pro Tools versions, including the 30-day trial. More information is at www.avid.com/pro-tools.

entry.summary: 2 minute read iZotope Photon: GPU stem separation, price, specs 2:52 iZotope's Photon uses multiple models on your GPU to split stems and clean up noisy audio. It's available now as a standalone app and ARA plugin. iZotope has launched Photon, a standalone app and ARA plugin for
entry.content:
2 minute read
iZotope Photon: GPU stem separation, price, specs
2:52

iZotope's Photon uses multiple models on your GPU to split stems and clean up noisy audio. It's available now as a standalone app and ARA plugin.

iZotope has launched Photon, a standalone app and ARA plugin for AI-powered stem separation and audio enhancement that uses 12 custom-trained models and runs locally on the GPU, with no uploads. Perhaps more significantly than that, for the long term at least, Photon is the first collaboration between the iZotope and Boris FX research teams.

It can split music into four stems, separate drums into individual elements [Handy for trying to work out what on earth Danny Carey is up to this time. Drumming Ed], isolate vocals, identify and separate speakers, and clean up noisy recordings. As an ARA plugin, it lets users run several models together and switch between them. Previews can start at any point in a clip. Model Manager downloads new and updated models without a reinstall.

Demix

  • Music 4 Stems: 4-stem separation model for music.
  • Music 4 Stems Ultra: new 4-stem separation model for music.
  • Drums 5 Stems: kick, snare, hi-hat, toms, and cymbals.
  • Voice Separator: splits up to 6 speakers from one audio file into individual stems.
  • Voice 2 Stems: voice and music.
  • Cinema 4 Stems: splits a video or audio file into dialogue, music, sound effects, and everything else.

Denoise

  • Voice Restore: handles speech, noise, levels, mic tone, and reverb.
  • Indoor / Indoor Noisy: reverb and room noise.
  • Outdoor / Outdoor Traffic / Outdoor Wind: models for traffic, urban noise, and heavy wind.

Formats and exports

Exports are WAV, FLAC, MP3, or video in the same format as the source, with the original video stream kept. Photon opens a lot too, namely .wav, .mp3, .flac, .aiff, .aif, .aac, .m4a, .mp4, .mkv, .mov, .mxf, and .mpg files. For video, it reads the audio track and can write the processed audio back.

Photon price and availability

Photon is available now at izotope.com/products/photon, with cyber deals through December 7, 2026. Prices are MSRP, with cyber prices in brackets.

  • Photon: $349 ($259)
  • Crossgrade from any paid iZotope product: $269 ($179)
  • Crossgrade from RX Elements (or any bundle that includes it): $199 ($129)
  • Crossgrade from RX Standard (or any bundle that includes it): $149 ($74)
  • Crossgrade from RX Advanced (or any bundle that includes it): $99 ($49)
  • Subscription: $19/month ($12 first month, then $19/month) or $119/year ($89 first year, then $119/year)

Photon requires macOS 14 or later on Apple silicon (Intel Macs are not supported), or Windows 10 or later, 64-bit, with a GPU of at least 4 GB VRAM. 16 GB of RAM is recommended and 8 GB is the minimum.

entry.title: DaVinci Resolve 21.2: new features and fixes
entry.summary: 4 minute read DaVinci Resolve 21.2: new features and fixes 7:20 DaVinci Resolve 21.2 supports MacBook Pro PROLED XDR touch screens and Gen 6 LUTs. Studio adds AI assistant tools, while Fusion Studio and Fairlight Live also update. Blackmagic Design's dev team has been hard at wor
entry.content:
4 minute read
DaVinci Resolve 21.2: new features and fixes
7:20

DaVinci Resolve 21.2 supports MacBook Pro PROLED XDR touch screens and Gen 6 LUTs. Studio adds AI assistant tools, while Fusion Studio and Fairlight Live also update.

Blackmagic Design's dev team has been hard at work as usual, and DaVinci Resolve 21.2 was uploaded to its servers overnight.

Because the company often works closely with Apple, this software update adds support for Apple MacBook Pro laptops with PROLED XDR displays as well as up to 5x faster rendering for M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon chips. This update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks (we covered the Gen 6 release here), as well as source timecode for extracted audio files. There are also fixes for network drive audio issues with some MXF clips and for AAF audio timecode accuracy from interlaced media, plus OGraf template loading and render fixes.

The paid DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 version, which is still 20% off at $236 until November 20, adds a few further tweaks, mainly in the AI assistant area. You can find the full list of its additional features below.

Fusion Studio 21.2 adds OGraf and Text+ fixes

Fusion Studio 21.2 has also been updated. Blackmagic says it improves stability, with fixes for custom tool control naming, Text+ CLS border extension anchoring, and OGraf template loading and rendering. The OGraf inspector now shows up to 35 template properties.

Fairlight Live 1.1.1 supports two new control panels

And finally, the new Fairlight Live 1.1.1 release adds support for Fairlight Live Audio Panel 20 and Fairlight Live Audio Panel 40. Blackmagic's control surfaces now cover 10, 20, and 40 faders supported by 1, 2, and 4 touchscreens, and provide controls for layers, bus, matrix, aux, VCA, sub-masters, talkback, and more. Prices scale from $2415 to $8245.

The latest software also includes templates for new ATEM Constellation IP switchers, improves audio I/O management and error reporting, and adds user-defined screen mapping and a panel screensaver after a period of inactivity.

All downloads are free and available from the Blackmagic Design Support Center.

Full release notes for each package

Here's the full list of new features and fixes per package.

entry.title: Affinity for iPad: what’s free and what’s missing

entry.content:
1 minute read
Affinity for iPad: what’s free and what’s missing
2:22

Affinity for iPad is free for individuals and combines sketching, vector, photo, and layout tools in one app.

Canva might be in some difficulty and relocating or laying off 22% of its workforce, but there's also new software to talk about. After being free on Mac and Windows since 2025, Canva's Affinity, an all-in-one app for professional design, photo editing, page layout, and sketching, has arrived on iPad. It's purpose-built for touch and, unlike most of its rivals, is a free download from the App Store.

The main caveat is that a Canva account is required to run it. The core tools are free for individuals, and Affinity's free tier contains a lot of functionality, so you only need to cross the company's palm with silver if you want the AI tools.

The app is built around Sketch, Vector, Pixel, and Layout studios. Sketch Studio includes over 350 editable brushes that respond to Apple Pencil pressure, tilt, and barrel roll. Photo tools cover non-destructive editing, composites, selections, and RAW development. Layout handles documents from short brochures to 500-page books, with print-ready output. The app works offline, and a single .af file holds a whole project and is shared with desktop.

Compatibility

Compatibility can be an Achilles' heel for software in this space, but Affinity seems to have it covered. It opens PSD, AI, INDD, IDML, PDF, SVG, and other formats, and exports to JPEG, PNG, WebP, PDF, SVG, EPUB, and INDD, with direct export to Canva. INDD and IDML imports preserve page structure, text frames, and basic styles, but GREP styles, anchored objects, and tables may need manual adjustment. Illustrator files need PDF compatibility enabled, and appearance stacks, masks, and advanced effects may flatten. Layered PSDs open with masks, groups, and adjustments in most cases, though smart objects and advanced filters may flatten.

Still to come

Canva AI Studio tools such as noise clearing, blur rescue, and background removal need a Canva premium plan. Affinity says content in the app is not used to train AI features.

As it stands, some features from the desktop version are not in the iPad version at launch: Books, Batch, Data Merge, Quick Adjustments, the Info and Scope panels, macro recording, and Astrophotography Studio. Free updates are promised, so hopefully they will arrive soon.

entry.content:
1 minute read
Canon EOS C400, C80, C50 firmware: new features
2:46

Canon's free December firmware adds Multi-Matrix color control to the EOS C400, C80, and C50. The C50 also gains Speedlite flash support.

Canon has announced a wide-ranging firmware update for the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50 on November 4, 2026.

Multi-Matrix color control and broadcast tools

The firmware update adds Multi-Matrix support across all three cameras, providing control over image color and saturation across selected color axes. Canon says this allows greater precision when matching multiple cameras and working with LED volumes, and helps cameras fit into existing real-time color workflows.

Supporting broadcast and virtual production environments is a bit of a focus with this update, with new features including improved CV metadata for focus and zoom encoder data, black level adjustment when shooting in Canon Log 2 or Canon Log 3, and image stabilization support for lenses exceeding 1000mm. Audio output in Slow & Fast mode is also supported, with Canon citing productions that move between high-speed sports footage and post-match interviews.

Autofocus and slow-motion 

For professional filmmakers using the EOS C400 and EOS C80, the update extends autofocus support in Slow & Fast mode to additional frame rates between 60p and 120p, including 72p, 75p, 90p, and 96p. This allows users to benefit from Canon's autofocus tracking across a wider range of slow-motion shooting scenarios.

The update also improves on-screen display information, including base ISO and fan indicators.

Speedlite flash support for EOS C50

The firmware update adds support for compatible Canon Speedlite flash accessories on the EOS C50 via the Multi-Function Accessory Shoe. This is aimed at professional photographers and hybrid shooters, including wedding and event creators, who want to capture still images using flash alongside video footage from the same event.

Supported accessories include EL-series and EX-series Speedlites, Macro Lights, and Speedlite Transmitters.

Customization and control

The update introduces additional customization options for RF lens buttons, camera control dials, and assignable buttons across the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50. Users can assign quick access to more functions, including autofocus, digital tele-converter, sensor mode, and exposure settings.

Availability

The new firmware updates for the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50 will be available to download free of charge from December 2026 via Canon support.
